_readme: HAND-MAINTAINED. This is the data behind the 'What the world owns' block on markets.html.
Nothing fetches it. Every figure here was read from the named publisher by a human or an
agent and carries its own as-of date, because the rows are NOT simultaneous.
THE COLUMN IS YEAR-OVER-YEAR, changed from month-over-month on 2026-08-16.
The reason is cadence, not preference. This block bakes on the MONTHLY tier, so a figure
whose freshness is measured in days is stale before the next bake even runs. Every row here
now carries a value and a change drawn from releases on a schedule the block can actually
keep up with. Four of the six rows could not carry an honest month-over-month at all; all
six can carry a year-over-year.
RULES FOR EDITING THIS FILE:
1. Never carry a figure forward. If a publisher has not updated, leave the old asOf date.
2. yoy is a genuine published-or-computable one-year percent, or null. Never zero, never
interpolated. null renders as an em dash.
3. yoySource says WHOSE number it is. Where the publisher prints the percentage itself, say
so and use theirs. Where we computed it, say that in yoyNote — standing rule 2.
4. yoyApprox: true renders a leading approximately-sign. Use it when the inputs are rounded
hard enough that a two-decimal answer would be false precision — standing rule 18.
5. THE VALUE AND THE CHANGE MUST COME FROM THE SAME SERIES. Two rows were realigned on
2026-08-16 for exactly this: money funds moved off ICI's weekly estimate onto ICI's
monthly Trends table, and crypto moved off a spot read of CoinGecko's global chart onto
CoinGecko's quarter-end report. Both now have a value and a change from one publication.
6. Gold is stored as tonnes x price, both years, and DERIVED at render time, so the
arithmetic is ours and is stated as ours. Do not replace it with a hardcoded total.
7. Anything you cannot verify goes in `omitted` with the reason, not in `rows` with a guess.

rows.label: Real estate
rows.universe: All global real estate — residential, commercial and agricultural
rows.yoyNote: Savills publishes this change itself — "a slight decline of 0.5% in 2024" — so it covers exactly the year the value is dated to. Note the series is not annual: editions exist for end-2017, end-2020, end-2022 and end-2024, and there is no end-2023 total to compare against directly.

rows.label: Listed shares
rows.universe: Market value of all domestic listed companies on WFE member exchanges — a total listed measure, not a free-float investable one
rows.yoySource: our calculation from WFE's own regional figures
rows.yoyNote: WFE prints no global year-over-year. Dividing this month's total by the same month last year gives +30.5%, which is wrong — exchange coverage changed. WFE's own regional year-over-year columns (Americas +22.9%, APAC +25.3%, EMEA +13.1%) imply a like-for-like global figure near +22%, and that is what is shown.

rows.label: Bonds
rows.universe: Global fixed income outstanding — the stock of debt, not the year's issuance
rows.yoyNote: SIFMA publishes this change itself: global fixed income outstanding rose 10.6% to $160.7 trillion in 2025, from $145.3 trillion at the end of 2024. Part of the rise is the dollar translating non-dollar debt, not new borrowing.

rows.label: Gold
rows.universe: Every ounce ever mined and still above ground — jewelry, bars, coins, funds and central bank reserves
rows.source: World Gold Council × World Bank price
rows.yoyNote: Both halves moved, and the price did nearly all of it: the above-ground stock grew 1.7% (216,265 to 219,891 metric tons) while the World Bank's monthly average price rose 22.0% ($3,340 to $4,073 a troy ounce). This is our own arithmetic, not a published total.

rows.label: US money market funds
rows.universe: Total net assets in US money market funds at month end. This is the closest published stand-in for parked cash and it is US-only — it is not global cash
rows.yoySource: both endpoints published by ICI in one table
rows.yoyNote: ICI's monthly Trends table prints June 2026 and June 2025 side by side — $7,900.4 billion against $7,023.8 billion. ICI's weekly release runs about six weeks fresher but keeps only three weeks of history, so it cannot supply a matching figure a year earlier; this block bakes monthly, so a month-end series is the right one to sit on.

rows.label: Crypto
rows.universe: Total market capitalization of all tracked cryptocurrencies, at quarter end
rows.yoySource: our calculation from two CoinGecko reports
rows.yoyNote: CoinGecko publishes a total only at quarter end: $2.1 trillion at 30 June 2026 against $3.5 trillion a year earlier. Both are rounded to one decimal, so the true change sits in a band around 40% rather than on it — hence the approximately sign. This is the one row on the chart whose value can move by a fifth before the next quarter closes.

omitted.label: Silver
omitted.reason: There is no authoritative figure for above-ground silver. The Silver Institute puts it at 19.3 billion ounces counting bullion and fabricated products, as of end-2023. CPM Group puts it near 1.7 million metric tons — roughly three times larger — counting jewelry, decorative objects and industrial products too, as of 2018. They are not measuring the same thing, and a single bar would have to pick one and hide that. The silver price is solid; the stock it multiplies is not.

omitted.label: Commodities
omitted.reason: Oil, wheat and copper are consumed rather than held, so there is no stock of value to total. Nobody publishes a figure worth citing, and inventing one to fill the row would be worse than the gap.

omitted.label: Art and collectibles
omitted.reason: The often-quoted art figure of about $59.6 billion is one year's turnover, not the value of the art in the world. It belongs on a different chart. Nobody publishes a total value for the world's art, watches, wine or cards.
